extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, aesthetics, and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative standards drawn from a scholarly treatment of Aristotle's Poetics about what counts as the proper end, form, and merit of poetry and the fine arts, especially tragedy. Focuses on criteria for plot, character, audience, and the relation of art to morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of art: realization of its own idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Art attains its end not through some external effect but in realising its own idea; the end of an object is inherent in that object and is reached when it has achieved its specific excellence and fulfils the law of its own being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with views that treat art's purpose as producing purely subjective or external effects; aligns with the conception of fine art as 'the revelation of the beautiful in external form.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's end as a distinctive, proper pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of art (for Aristotle) is a state of feeling — a pleasure which is distinctive of that art; each kind of poetry carries with it a distinctive pleasure which is the criterion by which the work is judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though the end is a subjective impression, it is grounded in human nature and so acquires objective validity; the 'pleasure which is distinctive of the art' is not accidental but inherent in the object that calls it forth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of taste: the cultivated public (ideal spectator)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appreciation of art is submitted to a man of sound aesthetic instincts (a cultivated public) who becomes 'the standard and the law' of taste; Aristotle distrusts just specialists and prefers the verdict of a cultivated popular judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between lower and higher audiences (e.g., 'free and educated listener' vs 'vulgar sort'); the ideal spectator's pleasure is the end of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic function: evoke pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar pleasurable effect of tragedy arises from the union of pity and fear; a tragic action must have an inherent capacity of calling forth pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test of artistic merit in a tragedy is the degree to which it fulfils this distinctive function; Aristotle's rules for plot, character, recognition, etc., flow from the requirement to elicit these emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry judged by its own laws (poetic truth ≠ scientific/moral truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry must be judged by its own laws, its own fundamental assumptions, and not by alien standards such as those of political science, morality, or natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct reply to Plato — poetic representation (myth, story) can have a place despite not conforming to literal truth; poetic and scientific kinds of truth differ in aim and standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of vice only by necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of moral depravity is excused only when demanded by inner necessity arising out of the structure of a piece (i.e., when it is required by the plot); gratuitous wickedness is forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vice may be subservient to the plot as one of 'those things demanded by the cogent necessity of dramatic motive'; otherwise avoid gratuitous immoral actions (Menelaus example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be 'good' or elevated (heroic goodness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and tragic poetry represent characters that have a kind of goodness—often 'heroic' or noble—which is distinct from ordinary virtue; comedy represents men as worse than life, tragedy as better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses traditional moral terms but the 'goodness' required is often an elevated or idealised quality that impresses the imagination (examples: Homeric heroes, Polygnotus' idealisation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero defined by aesthetic function, not ethical ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of the ideal tragic hero is deduced from the need to call forth the blended emotions of pity and fear; this characterization is driven by aesthetic effect rather than by an ethical model of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to specific prescriptions about plot construction and recognition scenes; ethical content is relevant only insofar as it contributes to the aesthetic total impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic excellence tied to capacity for effect (doing or suffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Aristotle the true nature of a thing can be expressed by what it is 'capable of doing or suffering'; in art, the effect produced on the percipient is treated as closely tied to the work's essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since work and effect are inseparable, describing a work in terms of the emotion it awakens is legitimate when referring to its excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and sequence of action leading to inevitable end
rubrics_metrics.description: A work's structure should exhibit unity and a closely linked sequence of acts which work up to an inevitable end; unity of plot and coherent sequence are central to artistic success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle praises Sophocles for the unity that pervades structure and the sequence that leads to an inevitable catastrophe; many of his formal rules for tragedy derive from this structural demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions and speech must accord with necessity or probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech or action must be interpreted in the light of all the circumstances (persons, occasion, end); if, from the study of these, the speech or action is in accordance with necessity or probability, then its artistic excellence is secured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morality enters only as implied in the aesthetic ideal; consistency with motive and circumstance preserves plausibility and artistic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of genres by moral/aesthetic type (comedy vs tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy aims at representing men as worse than in actual life (ludicrous deformity), while tragedy aims at representing men as better (heroic/elevated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This genre-differentiation explains different standards of character and the kinds of pleasure each genre seeks to produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral content secondary to aesthetic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's critical judgments rest on aesthetic and logical grounds rather than ethical aims; moral content matters only insofar as it affects the total impression and the distinctive pleasure of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even praise or blame (e.g., of Sophocles or Euripides) is based on unity, structure, character-drawing, and artistic functions rather than on didactic moral teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism and mere sentimentalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should not substitute mere 'troubling of the senses' or sensational details for genuine tragic emotion; sentimental or sensational means that merely disturb the senses debase tragic pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euripides is criticised for substituting sensory agitation (rags, tatters, trivial misery) for the true tragic emotion that arises from properly constructed action and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's educative role is conditional (suitable for children)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may serve a didactic or corrective moral purpose, especially in childhood education, but for grown men the poet's primary object is aesthetic: to produce elevated pleasure, not moral instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's restriction of poetry for moral education is resisted; the educative use of poetry does not determine its aesthetic standard for adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral greatness cannot wholly substitute for aesthetic grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: While poetic elevation may ennoble defective characters, Aristotle generally insists that moral goodness (goodness as such) is an important factor; greatness does not replace goodness (e.g., Satan would not be a fitting epic hero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle remains ambivalent between moral and aesthetic standards; the 'grandeur' demanded for art is ultimately tied to a morally intelligible form of greatness.
